The author defines this as love. How do you see this working in other relationships? Discuss. question 12 The Three Sisters of indigenous agriculture are corn, beans, and squash. These three plants together have fed generations of Native Americans throughout North and South America. The three are often planted together, and each enhances and supports the other plants. Can you think of other sacred plants that are intertwined with each other prevalent in other cultures? What is the value of such indigenous farming practices? question 13 Kimmerer talks about the importance of ceremonies to keep people grounded in their land and their community. Do you agree? What are the good and bad points of continuing age-old ceremonies? Should they be an important part of our lives? Kimmerer also recommends that the European colonizers should adopt ceremonies from their homelands and regenerate them to bond with the new lands. Would this work? Discuss. question 14 Kimmerer describes the childhood of her children and how she tried to raise them with proper regard and enjoyment for nature. However, her children experienced it in a way much different from her own, and she points out that is true for everyone. Do you think this applies to all other things? Do we all see things from a slightly different perspective than each other? Why, or why not? If yes, why should this be so? question 15 Kimmerer shares her experiences of teaching botany in unique ways, trying to get her students to understand the harmony of nature and to feel a connection to her gifts. She talks about her experiences in the Bible Belt and was thrilled to make a connection with the students. In what way do you think Christian students bond with the land in comparison to others? question 16 Kimmerer has written two books in recent years after she completed her Ph.D. These are Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses and Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants . Which one do you like better, and why? In what way are these two books similar and/or different from each other? question 17 Kimmerer is a Native American woman and a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. She is also a proponent of Traditional Ecological Knowledge. In what way do you think these factors color her work? Would her work be different if she did not have this background? Discuss. question 18 Kimmerer’s courses at the university include Land and Culture, Traditional Ecological Knowledge, Ethnobotany, Ecology of Mosses, Disturbance Ecology, and General Botany. How do you think she can teach the love of the land through these subjects? question 19 Kimmerer makes an effort to combine her scientific passion for plants, forests, and biology with her native Potawatomi heritage and knowledge. Why do you think she feels scientific and real understanding of the land are different? Do you think they are mutually exclusive? Discuss. question 20 Kimmerer grew up in a rural area where she interacted every day with plants in the garden, woods, or even the wetlands. This led to a deep and sustaining interest in the diverse biological world around her. How did this help her develop a relationship with nature? Do you think it is possible for everyone in the world to have this experience? Is this an entitled attitude? Discuss. question 21 The author has written two books: Gathering Moss: A Natural and Cultural History of Mosses , published in 2003, and Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants , published in 2013. Which of these two did you like the best, and why? question 22 Kimmerer received her bachelor’s and master’s degrees in botany. She also completed her Ph.D. in plant ecology and has an honorary M.Phil degree in Human Ecology. How have these studies helped her connect to nature in real life? In what ways has this education conflicted with the traditional knowledge of her people? question 23 The author’s grandfather, Asa Wall, was forcibly sent to the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and deliberately and systematically uprooted from his people and traditional way of life. How do you think these experiences have shaped the First Peoples’ psyche in the US and elsewhere? question 24 Kimmerer tries to recover her lost heritage by communicating more with her community’s elders and holders of knowledge and by learning the Potawatomi language. She also ensures that she attends certain ceremonial events and is an enrolled member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. Do you think it is possible to turn back time for these victims of colonization? Why, or why not? What are the different ways in which countries can help the First Peoples’ cultures thrive? question 25 The author is a proponent of Traditional Ecological Knowledge, which was first described by Fikret Berkes of the University of Manitoba as “a cumulative body of knowledge handed down through generations by cultural transmission, about the relationship of living beings with one another and with their environment.” What is this concept called in modern scientific language? Do you think this is something all humans have, or is it just a feature of the Native American culture? Can you think of other cultures that have developed such a relationship with nature? question 26 Kimmerer is also involved in projects involving helping her native Potawatomi tribe, the general Native American population, as well as the wider diaspora of non-white peoples in the USA. This includes sponsoring the Undergraduate Mentoring in Environmental Biology project, which helps non-white students by pairing them with faculty members. What do you think is the impact of such programs on minorities? In what way do you think such programs improve society as a whole? question 27 The author’s first job was as a microbiologist in Bausch & Lomb.
